mainTopic: Minor orphans and their father's debts, guarantors (ערב and קבלן) for loans and for a כתובה, and a dying man's claim of debt after giving his property to הקדש.
overview: Earlier on the daf, רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע both said that minor orphans do not pay their father's debt right away, but for different reasons. The גמרא finds the practical difference: when we know the father never paid, because he admitted the debt or died under a שמתא. The Sages of ארץ ישראל rule like רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע. A ברייתא about a guarantor who collects from minor orphans challenges רב פפא, and the גמרא answers that the words 'התקבלתי' make it a special case. Next come a story about a guarantor for a non-Jewish lender and a debate over the worry about 'bundles' (צררי). Then the גמרא turns to the משנה's rule about a guarantor for a כתובה. It tells how אביי suggested a divorce plan to help the poor scholar רב הונא, a plan that failed because he was a כהן. From that story the גמרא sets out which guarantors are bound and rules that an ordinary guarantor of a כתובה is never bound. Finally, רב הונא rules that a dying man who gave everything to הקדש is believed about a debt, and רב נחמן begins to challenge him. That discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two reasons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks when the two reasons for not making minor orphans pay would actually lead to different results. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both אמוראים give the same ruling: the minor orphans do not pay now. Their reasons are different, though. רב פפא's reason is a מצוה that minors are not obligated in, and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע's reason is a worry that the father already paid. The גמרא wants a case where only one of these reasons still applies.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?
Orphans who are still minors
Paying back a creditor is a מצוה (רב פפא's reason)

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?
phrases.notes: "Them" means רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע from just before this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the two reasons given earlier on the daf, before this section begins.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where the two reasons lead to different rulings.

steps.title: Two cases where we know the father did not pay
steps.stepSummary: The two opinions differ when the father admitted he still owed the money, or when he died under a שמתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is when the one who owed admits the debt. Or also: when they put him in שמתא and he died while still in his שמתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two cases where the worry that the father already paid disappears. In these cases רב פפא still lets the minors off, but רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע would make them pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the father admitted the debt, or died under a שמתא because he refused to pay, then we know the debt was never paid. That removes רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע's reason for letting the orphans off, so they must pay. רב פפא's reason has nothing to do with whether the father paid; minors are simply not obligated in the מצוה, so they still do not pay.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
The one who owed admits he still owes
They put him under a שמתא (a ban from the community)
Alternatively; or also

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
when the one who owed admits.
phrases.notes: This means the father himself admitted before he died that he had not paid yet.

phrases.english: Or also: when they put him under a ban,
and he died while still under his ban.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: When it is clear the father never paid (he admitted the debt, or died under a שמתא), רב פפא still lets the minors off, but רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע makes them pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: These cases show that the two reasons really are different, and they prepare the ground for the ruling in the next step.

steps.title: The Sages of ארץ ישראל rule like רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע
steps.stepSummary: A ruling sent from ארץ ישראל: if the father died under a שמתא, the הלכה follows רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent from there: if they put him under a ban and he died while still under his ban, the הלכה follows רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע.
steps.whatsHappening: The Sages of ארץ ישראל send a practical ruling for the שמתא case. The הלכה follows רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע, so the orphans must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ruling settles one of the two cases from step 2 in favor of רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע. It means that once we know the debt was not paid, the orphans do not get off just because they are minors. That goes against רב פפא's reason.

keyTerms.meaning: They sent from there, meaning from the Sages of ארץ ישראל to בבל
The final practical ruling (הלכה)

steps.whatToRemember: If the father died under a שמתא for not paying, the minor orphans must pay, following רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע.

phrases.english: They sent from there:
phrases.notes: "There" means ארץ ישראל. Its Sages sent rulings to the Sages in בבל.

phrases.english: If they put him under a ban and he died while still under his ban,

phrases.aramaic: הִלְכְתָא כְּרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ.
phrases.english: the הלכה follows רב הונא, son of רב יהושע.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical ruling for the second case described in step 2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In the שמתא case the orphans pay, following רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the father died under a שמתא, the הלכה follows רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע.

steps.title: A challenge from a ברייתא about a guarantor holding the loan document
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: a guarantor who holds the loan document cannot collect, but if the document says "I received from you," he can collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: a guarantor who has a loan document coming out from under his hand cannot collect. But if it is written in it "I received from you," he can collect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge the discussion. The ברייתא is about a guarantor who wants to be paid back after the debtor has died and left minor orphans. Step 5 explains why this is a difficulty, and step 6 answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A guarantor who simply holds the loan document cannot collect from the minor orphans. But if the lender wrote in it "I received from you," the guarantor can collect even from minor orphans. That ending is the problem: רב פפא says minors are never obligated to pay their father's debt.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantor for a loan
A loan document
"I received payment from you" (written by the lender)
Collects the money

steps.confusionAlert: "You" in "I received from you" is the guarantor, not the borrower. The lender is writing that the guarantor is the one who paid him.

phrases.english: They challenged:
A guarantor who had a loan document
coming out from under his hand,
phrases.notes: In other words, the guarantor is holding the loan document and claims he already paid the lender.

phrases.english: cannot collect.
But if it is written in it: "I received from you,"
he can collect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ruling in step 3, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that challenges the discussion about minor orphans.
steps.kashyaTarget: Apparently רב פפא's reason that minors are not obligated in the מצוה of paying a debt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lets the guarantor collect from the minor orphans when the document proves he paid. That suggests minors can be made to pay, and the only thing stopping collection is doubt about whether the debt was paid.

steps.title: The ברייתא fits רב הונא but is hard for רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lets a guarantor collect from orphans in some case. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע can explain that case, but רב פפא cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works for רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע: the case is when the debtor admitted he still owed. But for רב פפא it is a difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out why the ברייתא from the last step is a problem. It works with one opinion and not with the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע says orphans sometimes must pay, for example when the father admitted he had not paid yet. So he can explain the ברייתא as that case. רב פפא says young orphans never pay the father's debt right away, so the ברייתא seems to argue with him.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / it works well for
You can find a case for it
Admits that he still owes
It is a difficulty

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ –
phrases.english: Granted, according to Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua,
you can find the case: when the one who owed admits,
phrases.notes: 'The one who owed' is the father who died. He admitted before he died that he had not paid yet.

phrases.english: but according to Rav Pappa, it is difficult!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא quoted in step 4 is a challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's view that young orphans do not pay their father's debt right away.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lets a guarantor collect in some case. Only רב הונא's view leaves room for such a case.

steps.title: Writing 'I received' makes it a real loan document
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is a special case. The lender wrote 'הִתְקַבַּלְתִּי' for the guarantor, so the guarantor now holds a proper document.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there. That is exactly why the lender bothered to write 'I received' for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רב פפא. The case in the ברייתא is special because of the words 'I received.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the lender writes 'הִתְקַבַּלְתִּי' (I received payment from you), the loan document now belongs to the guarantor, as if the debt were written to him. Even רב פפא agrees that a debt backed by a written document can be collected from the orphans. So the ברייתא does not argue with him.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
He took the trouble
'I received' payment

steps.whatToRemember: רב פפא stands. The guarantor collects in the ברייתא only because 'הִתְקַבַּלְתִּי' turned the document into his own.

phrases.english: It is different there,
for this reason he took the trouble and wrote for him "I received."
phrases.notes: The lender wrote this for the guarantor so the guarantor could use the document to collect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a special case (the document says 'I received').
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the ברייתא lets a guarantor collect from orphans even without a document of his own.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'I received' wording gives the guarantor a written debt, which even רב פפא allows him to collect.

steps.title: A guarantor for a non-Jewish lender: no worry about bundles
steps.stepSummary: A guarantor paid a non-Jewish lender before the lender claimed from the orphans. רב מרדכי quotes רבא: with a non-Jewish lender we do not worry that the father already paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: A guarantor paid a non-Jewish lender before the lender claimed from the orphans. רב מרדכי told רב אשי in the name of רבא: even the one who worries about 'bundles' only means a Jewish lender. A non-Jewish lender goes straight to the guarantor, so we do not worry about bundles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story and brings רבא's ruling, which favors the guarantor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry of צררי is that the father may have quietly handed the lender bundles of money before he died. With a non-Jewish lender, the lender may go straight to the guarantor. So the father would not pay early and risk the lender collecting twice. Without that worry, the guarantor can collect from the orphans.

keyTerms.meaning: Guarantor
Orphans
We are concerned
Bundles of money

steps.confusionAlert: Here the 'bundles' are a possible early payment by the father. In the next step רב אשי treats them as security given at the start of the loan.

phrases.english: There was a certain guarantor for a gentile's loan
who repaid the gentile
before he claimed from the orphans.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the gentile lender. The borrower had died, and now the guarantor wants his money back from the orphans.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי לְרַב אָשֵׁי,
phrases.english: Rav Mordekhai said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי אָמַר אֲבִימִי מֵהַגְרוֹנְיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא:
phrases.english: So said Avimi of Hagronya in the name of Rava:
Even according to the one who says we are concerned about bundles,
phrases.notes: 'Bundles' means money the dead father might have secretly handed the lender.

phrases.english: that applies to a Jewish lender;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל גּוֹי, כֵּיוָן דְּבָתַר עָרְבָא אָזֵיל –
phrases.english: but a gentile, since he goes after the guarantor,
we are not concerned about bundles.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new story about guarantors and orphans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With a non-Jewish lender we do not worry about bundles, because he can go straight to the guarantor.

steps.title: רב אשי: with a non-Jewish lender, bundles are even more likely
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי flips the reasoning. Since a non-Jewish lender goes straight to the guarantor, no one would guarantee such a loan unless the borrower first gave the lender bundles as security.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: On the contrary! Even the one who does not worry about bundles only means a Jewish lender. With non-Jewish lenders, who go straight to the guarantor, the guarantor would not have agreed unless the borrower gave bundles from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי rejects רב מרדכי's reasoning and turns it upside down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב מרדכי used the fact that a non-Jewish lender goes after the guarantor to remove the worry about bundles. רב אשי uses the same fact to say the worry is stronger. A guarantor facing such a lender would agree only if the borrower had already put bundles of money in the lender's hands at the start.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary
Their law
He placed it in his hands (as security)
From the start

steps.whatToRemember: The same fact, that a non-Jewish lender goes straight to the guarantor, leads רב מרדכי to 'no worry about bundles' and רב אשי to 'surely there were bundles.'

phrases.english: He said to him: On the contrary!

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לָא חָיְישִׁינַן לִצְרָרֵי –
phrases.english: Even according to the one who says we are not concerned about bundles,
that applies to a Jewish lender;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל גּוֹיִם, כֵּיוָן דְּדִינַיְיהוּ בָּתַר עָרְבָא אָזְלִי,
phrases.english: but gentiles, since their law goes after the guarantor,
if the borrower had not put bundles in the lender's hands from the start,
the guarantor would not have accepted it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects and reverses the reasoning of step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole claim that a non-Jewish lender removes the worry about bundles.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Because a non-Jewish lender goes straight to the guarantor, a guarantor would agree only if security had been given, so bundles are more likely, not less.

steps.title: Quoting the next line of the משנה about a guarantor for a כתובה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new section by quoting רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's rule in the משנה about a ערב for a woman's כתובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: And so רבן שמעון בן גמליאל used to say: someone who is a guarantor for a woman's כתובה, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה to start discussing it. This sets up the story that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל rules that if a ערב backs a woman's כתובה and her husband divorces her, the husband must vow never to benefit from her. The worry is that a couple could fake a divorce to squeeze money out of the guarantor and then get back together. The vow blocks that trick.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantor: someone who promises to pay if the main person does not
The marriage contract that promises the wife money if she is divorced or widowed
'And so on.' The rest of the quote is in the משנה

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן הָיָה רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: And so Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would say:
A guarantor for a woman for her marriage contract, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points to the rest of the משנה: the divorcing husband must vow not to benefit from her, so he can never remarry her.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הָיָה רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, moving from a guarantor of an ordinary loan to a guarantor of a כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a ערב backs a כתובה, the divorcing husband must vow off benefit from his wife, so he cannot remarry her.

steps.title: אביי suggests a divorce plan to help a poor scholar
steps.stepSummary: משה בר עצרי guaranteed his daughter-in-law's כתובה. His son רב הונא was poor. אביי suggests that רב הונא divorce his wife so she can collect from the father, and then remarry her.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה בר עצרי was a guarantor for his daughter-in-law's כתובה. His son, רב הונא, was a young Torah scholar who was short on money. אביי said: Isn't there someone who could go and advise רב הונא to divorce his wife? Then she would collect her כתובה from his father, and afterwards רב הונא could marry her again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real story connected to our משנה. אביי proposes a plan that uses the guarantee to get money for a poor son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the father was the ערב, a divorce would force the father to pay the כתובה. The money would come into the son's household, and the couple would then reunite. This is exactly the kind of plan the משנה's vow is meant to prevent, which sets up רבא's objection.

keyTerms.meaning: A young Torah scholar
His daughter-in-law
Advice
He would take her back (remarry her)

phrases.english: Moshe bar Atzri
was a guarantor for the marriage contract of his daughter-in-law.
Rav Huna, his son,
was a young Torah scholar,
and things were tight for him.
Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: לֵיכָּא דְּנֵיזִיל דְּנַסְּבֵיהּ עֵצָה לְרַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: Is there no one who will go and give advice to Rav Huna,
that he should divorce his wife,
and she will go and collect the marriage contract from his father,
phrases.notes: 'His father' is משה בר עצרי, the guarantor.

phrases.english: and then he should take her back?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹשֶׁה בַּר עַצְרִי עָרְבָא דִּכְתוּבְּתַהּ דְּכַלָּתֵיהּ הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life case connected to the משנה just quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי suggests a divorce so the wife can collect from the guarantor-father, with the couple remarrying afterwards.

steps.title: רבא objects: the משנה requires a vow that blocks remarriage
steps.stepSummary: רבא points out that the משנה requires the husband to vow off benefit from his wife, so the plan to remarry would fail.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: But we learned in the משנה, 'He must make her forbidden to himself by a vow'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges אביי's plan using the very משנה they are learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's vow exists to stop this exact trick. If רב הונא must vow never to benefit from his wife, he cannot remarry her, and the whole plan falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: He must make her forbidden to him by a vow, so he gets no benefit from her

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
But didn't we learn: 'He must make her forbidden to him by a vow'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's plan from step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's plan that רב הונא divorce and later remarry his wife.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה requires a vow when a ערב is involved, and that vow makes remarriage impossible.

steps.title: אביי answers: not every divorce happens in בית דין
steps.stepSummary: אביי replies that the vow is imposed by a court, and a divorce done privately would not involve it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Is that to say that everyone who divorces does it in בית דין?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends his plan against רבא's objection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vow in the משנה is something בית דין makes the husband take. If רב הונא divorced his wife privately, outside of בית דין, no one would make him vow, so he could still remarry her.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Is that to say...?' A way of rejecting an assumption
A court (בית דין)

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
Is that to say that everyone who divorces
divorces in a court?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ כֹּל דִּמְגָרֵשׁ בְּבֵי דִינָא מְגָרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's objection from step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the rule: the vow applies only when the divorce happens in בית דין.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא assumed every divorce would come with the vow, which would block remarriage.
steps.terutzMaskana: A divorce done privately avoids the court-imposed vow, so remarriage stays possible.

steps.title: The plan fails: רב הונא turns out to be a כהן
steps.stepSummary: It turns out רב הונא was a כהן, who may not remarry a divorced woman. אביי sighs: 'Poverty follows the poor.'
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end it came out that he was a כהן. אביי said: This is what people say: poverty follows the poor.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. The plan could never have worked, and אביי comments on it with a popular saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן may not marry a divorced woman, even his own ex-wife. So once רב הונא divorced, he could never take her back, and the plan was impossible. אביי's saying means that a poor person keeps running into more bad luck.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter was revealed / it came out
A priest, who may not marry a divorced woman
Poverty follows the poor

steps.whatToRemember: אביי's plan worked on paper (divorce outside בית דין, then remarry), but it failed in practice because רב הונא was a כהן.

phrases.english: In the end the matter was revealed
that he was a priest.
phrases.notes: A כהן can't marry a divorced woman, even his own ex-wife, so he could never take her back.

phrases.english: Abaye said,
This is what people say:
Poverty follows the poor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story: the plan defended in step 12 turns out to be impossible.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Because רב הונא was a כהן, he could not remarry a divorcée, so the divorce plan could not help him.

steps.title: Would אביי really give such advice? He calls it wicked elsewhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי: he himself said that someone who advises selling property under רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's rule is a 'רשע ערום'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did אביי really say this? But אביי himself said: Who is a 'cunning wicked person'? Someone who gives advice to sell property following רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions how אביי could suggest the divorce plan, since he elsewhere condemns giving advice like this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Elsewhere, אביי calls it wicked to advise someone to use a legal loophole that cuts another person out of what he was meant to get. The divorce plan seems similar: it uses the law to force the father to pay. So אביי seems to contradict himself.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Did he really say this?' Introduces a contradiction
A cunning wicked person
One who gives advice

phrases.english: But did Abaye really say this?
But didn't Abaye say:
Who is a 'cunning wicked person'?
This is one who gives advice

phrases.aramaic: לִמְכּוֹר בִּנְכָסִים כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל!
phrases.english: to sell property according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel!
phrases.notes: This is the case where property goes to one person and after him to another. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל lets the first one sell it, cutting out the second.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר אַבָּיֵי הָכִי וְהָא אָמַר אַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to אביי's suggestion in step 10 and challenges whether it fits with his own teaching.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's suggestion to advise רב הונא to divorce in order to collect from his father.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אביי calls someone who advises using a legal loophole against another person a 'רשע ערום', yet here he himself suggests such advice.

steps.title: A son and a Torah scholar are different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 14. Getting money from a father for his own son, who is a Torah scholar, is not the scheming that אביי condemned.
steps.simpleTranslation: His son is different, and a Torah scholar is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends אביי's advice to רב הונא. It explains why that advice does not make אביי a 'רשע ערום' by his own standard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי had called someone a 'רשע ערום' for advising a scheme that gets money out of another person. Here the money goes from a father to his own son, and that son is a Torah scholar who needs support to learn. So pushing the father to pay is not considered wicked.

keyTerms.meaning: Is different. A case is set apart from the general rule.
A young Torah scholar.
A cunning wicked person, someone who schemes legally.

phrases.english: His son is different,
and a Torah scholar is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the קשיא of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the special relationship (son) and status (scholar) remove the problem of scheming.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי's advice looked like the very scheming he himself condemned.
steps.terutzMaskana: Getting money from a father for his scholar son is not wickedness.

steps.title: A guarantor of a כתובה is not obligated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a new problem with the story. משה בר עצרי was only a guarantor, and a guarantor of a כתובה is not obligated to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he was a guarantor, and we hold that a guarantor of a כתובה is not obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about the story. Why would the wife be able to collect from the father at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's whole plan depended on the wife collecting her כתובה from משה בר עצרי. But the accepted rule is that a regular ערב for a כתובה does not become obligated. If so, the plan should never have worked.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantor who promises to pay if the borrower does not.
We hold this as the accepted rule.
Becomes legally bound to pay.

phrases.english: But wasn't he a guarantor,
and we hold
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have these words; the square brackets show they belong in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: a guarantor of a כתובה is not obligated!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the moral question to a legal question about the same story.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption in step 10 that the wife could collect from משה בר עצרי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A regular guarantor of a כתובה is not bound to pay, so the father would owe nothing.

steps.title: He was an unconditional guarantor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that משה בר עצרי was a קבלן, a stronger kind of guarantor who is bound.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was an unconditional guarantor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question in short. The father was not a regular ערב but a קבלן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קבלן takes on the debt more directly than a regular ערב. Because of this, he is obligated even for a כתובה. That is why the wife could collect from the father.

keyTerms.meaning: An unconditional guarantor. The creditor can collect from him directly.

phrases.english: He was an unconditional guarantor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: he was a קבלן, not a regular ערב.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He was a plain ערב, who is not bound for a כתובה.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was a קבלן, who is bound.

steps.title: Problem according to the view that a קבלן needs the husband to have property
steps.stepSummary: The answer that he was a קבלן works for one opinion. But according to the view that a קבלן is bound only if the husband owns property, there is a problem, since רב הונא was poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says a קבלן of a כתובה is obligated even if the husband has no property. But for the one who says he is obligated only if the husband has property, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 17. It brings up a second opinion about when a קבלן of a כתובה is bound.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a disagreement about a קבלן for a כתובה. One opinion says he is bound even if the husband owns nothing, and by that opinion step 17 is fine. The other opinion says he is bound only if the husband owns property. רב הונא was poor, so by that opinion his father should not be bound.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well according to the one who says. It opens a challenge from another opinion.
Property.
What is there to say? This shows a real difficulty.

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says:
an unconditional guarantor of a כתובה

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֵית לֵיהּ נִכְסֵי לְבַעַל,
phrases.english: even though the husband has no property,
is obligated. It is fine.
But according to the one who says:
if he has property, the guarantor is obligated,
phrases.notes: 'He' means the husband. The question is whether the husband owns property.

phrases.english: if he does not have property, the guarantor is not obligated.
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 17 using a second opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that משה בר עצרי was a קבלן (step 17).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By one opinion, a קבלן is bound only if the husband owns property. רב הונא was poor, so the father would not be bound.

steps.title: First answer: he once had property that was lost
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא did own property when he married, so the guarantee took effect. The property was ruined later.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: he did have property, and it got ruined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first answer to step 18. רב הונא was not always poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the time of the marriage, רב הונא owned property. So even by the stricter opinion, the father's guarantee took effect then. The later loss of the property does not cancel the father's obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say. It introduces one of several possible answers.
It became blighted, meaning ruined or lost.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
he did have property,
and it got blighted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual reframing: there was property at the time of the guarantee.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא never had property, so the guarantee never took effect.
steps.terutzMaskana: He had property at the marriage, so the guarantee took effect, even though the property was lost later.

steps.title: Second answer: a father truly binds himself for his son
steps.stepSummary: Even by the stricter opinion, a father seriously commits himself to guarantee his son's כתובה, even when the son owns nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: a father, for his son, really obligates himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer to step 18. It is based on the father-son relationship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stricter opinion requires the husband to own property because a regular קבלן does not seriously mean to pay otherwise. A father, though, means it fully when he guarantees for his own son. So he is bound even if the son owns nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: He truly binds himself to pay.
A father toward his son.

steps.whatToRemember: משה בר עצרי had to pay because he was a קבלן. This holds either because רב הונא had property at the marriage, or because a father seriously binds himself for his son. And pushing a father to pay for his scholar son is not scheming.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
a father toward his son
really obligates himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, independent answer to the קשיא of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exception based on relationship: a father's commitment for his son is serious.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With no property, a קבלן's guarantee is not binding.
steps.terutzMaskana: A father fully binds himself for his son, even without property.

steps.title: The teaching about which guarantors are bound
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the source of the dispute from step 18. Everyone agrees about two cases, and there is a dispute about two others.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was stated: an ordinary guarantor of a כתובה is not bound, by all opinions. A קבלן of a loan is bound, by all opinions. A קבלן of a כתובה and an ordinary guarantor of a loan are in dispute. One opinion says he is bound only if the borrower (or husband) has property. The other says he is bound either way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the full teaching that step 18 was relying on. This shows exactly where the two opinions about a קבלן disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are four cases. A weak guarantee on a weak obligation (an עָרֵב of a כתובה) is never binding. A strong guarantee on a strong obligation (a קַבְּלָן of a loan) is always binding. The two middle cases, a קבלן of a כתובה and an עָרֵב of a loan, are in dispute, and the dispute depends on whether the main debtor owns property.

keyTerms.meaning: An ordinary guarantor, who pays only if the main debtor cannot.
A stronger guarantor, who can be asked to pay directly.
Is bound or obligated.
A creditor; here it means a loan.
They disagree.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two words. An עָרֵב is the weaker kind of guarantor and a קַבְּלָן is the stronger kind. That is why a קבלן of a כתובה is in dispute, while an עָרֵב of a כתובה is not bound by anyone.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is the background for steps 18 to 20. It explains why רב הונא's poverty was a problem only according to one opinion.

phrases.english: As it was stated:
phrases.notes: This is the source for the opinion mentioned back in step 18.

phrases.aramaic: עָרֵב דִּכְתוּבָּה – דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל לָא מִשְׁתַּעְבַּד.
phrases.english: A guarantor of a כתובה – all agree he is not bound.

phrases.aramaic: קַבְּלָן דְּבַעַל חוֹב – דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל מִשְׁתַּעְבַּד.
phrases.english: A קבלן of a loan – all agree he is bound.

phrases.aramaic: קַבְּלָן דִּכְתוּבָּה, וְעָרֵב דְּבַעַל חוֹב – פְּלִיגִי;
phrases.english: A קבלן of a כתובה, and a guarantor of a loan – they disagree;

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר: אִי אִית לֵיהּ נִכְסֵי לְלֹוֶה – מִשְׁתַּעְבַּד,
phrases.english: One Sage holds: if the borrower has property – he is bound,
phrases.notes: "Borrower" here also covers the husband in the כתובה case.

phrases.english: if he does not have – he is not bound;

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: בֵּין אִית לֵיהּ וּבֵין לֵית לֵיהּ – מִשְׁתַּעְבַּד.
phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: whether he has or does not have – he is bound.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source of the opinion that step 18 and step 20 discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עָרֵב of a כתובה is never bound and a קבלן of a loan is always bound. For a קבלן of a כתובה and an עָרֵב of a loan, one opinion says he is bound only if the debtor has property, and the other says he is bound either way.

steps.title: The final ruling on guarantors
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is that a guarantor is bound whether or not the debtor has property. The one exception is a guarantor of a כתובה, who is never bound.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is: a guarantor is bound whether the debtor has property or not. The exception is a guarantor of a כתובה. Even if the husband has property, that guarantor is not bound.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical ruling for the dispute it just quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הלכה follows the stricter opinion for an עָרֵב of a loan, so he is bound even if the borrower owns nothing. But an ordinary עָרֵב of a כתובה stays exempt in every case, even when the husband has property.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical הלכה, the final ruling.
Except for.
Even though.

steps.whatToRemember: In practice an עָרֵב is always bound, except for an עָרֵב of a כתובה, who is never bound.

phrases.english: And the הלכה is: a guarantor –

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין אִית לֵיהּ וּבֵין לֵית לֵיהּ, מִשְׁתַּעְבַּד;
phrases.english: whether he has or does not have property, is bound;
except for a guarantor of a כתובה –

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּאִית לֵיהּ לְבַעַל, לָא מִשְׁתַּעְבַּד.
phrases.english: for even though the husband has property, he is not bound.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute quoted in step 21.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A guarantor is bound whether or not the debtor has property, except a guarantor of a כתובה, who is never bound.

steps.title: Why is a guarantor of a כתובה exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the exception.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a guarantor of a כתובה is treated differently. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every other guarantor is bound. So the גמרא wants to know what is special about a guarantee on a כתובה.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the exception in step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a guarantor of a כתובה is not bound, even when the husband has property.

steps.title: He only did a מצוה, and she lost nothing
steps.stepSummary: The guarantor was only helping a marriage happen, and the wife did not hand over any money, so he is not bound.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was doing a מצוה, and he did not cause her to lose anything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two reasons why a guarantor of a כתובה is not bound.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First, he signed to help the marriage go forward, which is a מצוה, and did not really mean to take on a debt. Second, unlike a lender, the wife did not give out money because of his guarantee, so she lost nothing because of him.

keyTerms.meaning: A good deed; here, helping a marriage happen.
Caused her a loss.

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same as step 20. There the גמרא said a father does bind himself for his son's כתובה. This step is about an ordinary guarantor with no special closeness.

phrases.english: It is a מצוה that he did,
and he did not cause her to lose anything.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He guaranteed only to help with the מצוה of marriage, and the wife lost nothing because of his guarantee.

steps.title: A dying man who gave everything to הקדש is believed about a debt
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that a שכיב מרע who gave all his property to הקדש is believed when he says he owes someone a מנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: a dying man gave all his property to הקדש, and then said, "So-and-so has a מנה with me." He is believed. There is a חזקה that a person does not plot against הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב הונא gives a ruling about a dying man's claim that he owes money after giving everything to הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we might worry that the man is inventing a debt to send money to a friend. רב הונא says we trust him, because a person would not lie in a way that takes money away from הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is dangerously ill.
He gave property to הקדש, the Temple treasury.
A sum of one hundred זוז.
Believed.
A plot or scheme to cheat someone.
A firm assumption about how people behave.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
A dying man who consecrated all his property,
and said "So-and-so has a מנה in my hand" – he is believed;

phrases.aramaic: חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם עוֹשֶׂה קְנוּנְיָא עַל הֶקְדֵּשׁ.
phrases.english: there is a presumption that a person does not plot against הקדש.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the guarantor discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dying man who consecrated all his property is believed when he says he owes someone money, because a person does not plot against הקדש.

steps.title: רב נחמן challenges רב הונא from רב and שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן argues that a person also would not plot against his own children. Yet רב and שמואל do not believe a dying man about a debt unless he says "give." This shows a dying man may say such things for a different reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן challenged this: Does a person plot against his own children? Of course not. Yet רב and שמואל both said: if a dying man said "So-and-so has a מנה with me" and he said "give," they give. If he did not say "give," they do not give. So we see that a person tends to talk this way so that his sons will not seem rich.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן attacks רב הונא's reasoning. He shows that the trust given to the dying man in רב הונא's case does not hold up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as no one plots against הקדש, no one plots against his own children. Still, רב and שמואל ignore a dying man's claim of debt unless he says "give." That is because people say such things to hide their wealth, not to cheat anyone. So רב הונא's reason, that no one plots against הקדש, does not prove the debt is real.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged it.
Give!, an explicit instruction to pay.
So we see, apparently.
To make satisfied, here meaning to make his sons look wealthy.

steps.confusionAlert: רב נחמן is not saying the dying man is cheating anyone. His point is that a man may claim a debt that is not real just to hide his wealth, so the claim alone proves nothing.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman challenged it:

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי אָדָם עוֹשֶׂה קְנוּנְיָא עַל בָּנָיו?!
phrases.english: And does a person plot against his children?!
For Rav and Shmuel both say:
A dying man who said "So-and-so has a מנה in my hand";
if he said "give" – they give.
If he did not say "give" – they do not give.

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא אָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת בָּנָיו;
phrases.english: Apparently a person tends not to make his sons seem sated;
phrases.notes: "Sated" here means rich. He may claim debts so people won't think his sons are inheriting a lot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's ruling and reason in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's reason that the dying man is believed because no one plots against הקדש.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No one plots against his own children either, yet רב and שמואל do not believe a dying man's debt claim without "give." So such claims may be made just to hide wealth, and the no-plotting reason does not make the claim believable.
